strengths: The stopping condition has a clear practical interpretation: continue only when some point's posterior expected improvement exceeds its evaluation cost. The equivalence between the PBGI and LogEIPC formulations is elegant and makes the rule straightforward to implement without an additional threshold.

The paper studies an important and relatively underexplored aspect of Bayesian optimization. Cost-adjusted simple regret is an appropriate objective when evaluation cost and terminal solution quality are expressed in common units.

The evaluation covers model-matched Gaussian-process experiments, higher-dimensional numerical optimization, LCBench, and NATS-Bench. It includes varying and unknown costs, 50 seeds, uncertainty bars, multiple cost scales, and several established stopping baselines.

The proposed rule is empirically competitive, especially with PBGI and at high evaluation costs. The appendix usefully exposes failures under model mismatch rather than hiding them, including weaker results on CIFAR-100, ImageNet16-120, and unknown-cost Adult.

The manuscript is generally well organized and explains the relationship among Pandora's Box, PBGI, LogEIPC, and stopping behavior clearly. No material research-ethics concerns arise from the synthetic and public benchmark experiments, and LLM assistance is disclosed.
weaknesses: The proof of the central Theorem 2 is incomplete as written. Equations (18)-(19) establish only an upper bound on cumulative cost, yet the theorem bounds terminal simple regret plus cumulative cost. The missing step must explicitly combine the telescoping improvement with terminal regret. In addition, Equation (15) conditions on F_{t-1} but uses the post-observation quantity alpha_EI_t(x_t); it should use the posterior before selecting and observing x_t. The lemma and stopping-time indices have the same off-by-one problem. The intended result appears repairable, but the submitted proof does not establish the advertised theorem.

The theoretical statements are too broad for their assumptions. Compactness and a constant prior mean do not ensure existence of the PBGI root, acquisition optimizer, or even a measurable finite minimum for an arbitrary random function. Gaussian/nondegeneracy, sample-path regularity, measurability, and stopping/integrability conditions should be stated. The unknown-cost experiments also replace cost by a posterior expectation, but no guarantee is provided for realized stochastic costs.

The theoretical guarantee is weak: it only shows performance no worse in expectation than stopping immediately after initialization. It neither quantifies closeness to the Bayesian-optimal policy nor provides a useful regret rate. The argument is essentially one-step value accounting once expected improvement is at least cost, so claims of a major or first general theoretical guarantee should be moderated and positioned more carefully relative to existing EI and economic-selection stopping rules.

The evaluated algorithm differs materially from the analyzed rule. The paper introduces an unspecified stabilization period and debounce requirement, and the 8D experiments use a 20-iteration moving average. These changes can alter the stopping time and invalidate the stated guarantee. Exact stabilization/debounce settings and separate ablations of the unmodified rule are needed.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code or repository is provided, and important implementation details are missing, including the exact stabilization and debounce parameters. Some appendix cross-references are broken (for example, 'Figure ??'), and Table 1 says results are identical across acquisition functions despite reporting only one set, without enough explanation to verify that surprising claim.

The practical evidence remains somewhat narrow: only three selected datasets from each empirical benchmark are used, all experiments are noiseless, and the cost-to-objective conversion factor is selected to avoid degenerate regimes. Although multiple scales appear in the appendix, stronger sensitivity analysis and realistic justification for lambda are important because this user-specified conversion largely determines when the method stops. There is also no dedicated limitations discussion covering noise, batches, misspecified posteriors, or the consequences of using estimated costs.

strengths: Significance: Adaptive stopping under heterogeneous evaluation costs is a practically important and relatively underexplored aspect of Bayesian optimization. The cost-adjusted simple-regret objective directly captures the intended quality-versus-cost tradeoff.

Originality: The algebraic equivalence between the PBGI stopping condition and stopping when expected improvement does not exceed evaluation cost (Equations 6–10) gives a clean common interpretation for PBGI and LogEIPC, although the resulting rule itself is fairly natural.

Empirical breadth: The paper compares numerous acquisition–stopping-rule combinations, uses 50 seeds, and includes model-matched GP experiments, higher-dimensional experiments, LCBench, NATS-Bench, known and unknown costs, and several cost scales. The appendix usefully reports runtime and failure-to-stop behavior.

Presentation and ethics: The high-level motivation and organization are generally clear, figures communicate the main trends, and the authors disclose their LLM usage. The work raises no evident material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: Lemma 1 is internally inconsistent in its time indexing. It defines the posterior acquisition alpha_t after conditioning on observations through t, but claims this quantity justifies selecting x_t. In the noiseless setting, x_t has already been evaluated under that posterior and has zero expected improvement. The proof alternates among y*_{1:t}, y*_{1:t-1}, and x_t without resolving this contradiction (notably Equations 12–14). The intended claim likely concerns x_{t+1} and iterations t<tau, but that is not the theorem stated or proved.

Soundness: Theorem 2 inherits the same indexing error: Equation 15 conditions on F_{t-1} while equating the improvement from evaluating x_t with alpha_t, which is defined using F_t. Invoking the optional stopping theorem also lacks the required measurability/integrability justification. Moreover, the written proof ends after bounding cumulative cost in Equation 19; that bound alone does not prove the displayed cost-adjusted-regret bound because the remaining simple regret is omitted. A corrected telescoping argument may be possible, but the central advertised guarantee is not currently established.

Scope of theory versus implementation: The analysis assumes one initial evaluation and the exact stopping rule, whereas experiments start with 2(d+1) points and introduce an unspecified stabilization period, debounce mechanism, and, in 8D, a 20-step moving average. These modifications materially change the stopping time and are not covered by the theorem. Thus the theoretical claim does not validate the evaluated practical algorithm.

Reproducibility: No code or artifact link is provided, and essential implementation choices are missing, especially the stabilization length, debounce length, precise moving-average triggering convention, treatment of initial points in cost-adjusted regret, and sufficient acquisition-optimizer settings. The paper also contains apparent reporting inconsistencies, including the reference to a nonexistent “Figure ??” and ambiguity about empirical iteration caps.

Experimental validity: Table 1 states that failure-to-stop counts are identical across all four acquisition functions, even though those functions generate different observations and stopping statistics; this surprising assertion is neither explained nor broken down by acquisition function. Several baselines are altered or potentially disadvantaged—for example, SRGap-med is retuned only in empirical experiments, moving averaging is applied selectively, and KG is omitted—without sensitivity analyses establishing a fair comparison.

Evaluation reach: The real-data evidence covers only the first three datasets from LCBench-lite and three NATS-Bench datasets. Representative cost-conversion factors are explicitly selected to avoid degenerate regimes, while this conversion is central to the practical decision problem. Appendix sweeps help, but there is no principled user-preference study or robustness analysis for choosing lambda under model mismatch.

Significance and originality are overstated: The guarantee, even if repaired, only establishes performance no worse than stopping immediately under a correctly specified Bayesian model and matched acquisition rule. It provides neither a useful approximation to the Bayes-optimal policy in correlated settings nor a nontrivial regret rate. Since the stopping condition is essentially the one-step rule “continue iff expected improvement exceeds cost,” the conceptual advance is modest relative to the paper’s claims of a novel unified framework and the first guarantee of its type.

Limitations are not treated adequately. The paper acknowledges model mismatch in isolated experimental discussions, but it lacks a consolidated account of dependence on noiseless observations, correct GP specification, exact acquisition optimization, objective–cost unit conversion, and the gap between the analyzed and deployed stopping rules. These are central limitations, not peripheral extensions.

strengths: The stopping condition—continue only when some point's posterior expected improvement exceeds its evaluation cost—is intuitive, computationally simple, and practically relevant. Its equivalence under the PBGI and LogEIPC formulations provides a useful unifying perspective, although the algebra itself is fairly direct.

The empirical study is broad: it covers model-matched 1D and 8D synthetic problems, varying cost landscapes and scales, LCBench, NATS-Bench, known and unknown costs, and cost-model mismatch. Comparisons include numerous adaptive rules, immediate stopping, and hindsight references, with 50 seeds and uncertainty bars.

The results generally support the practical claim that the proposed rule, especially with PBGI, achieves favorable cost-adjusted regret and avoids the excessive sampling exhibited by several baselines. Runtime measurements also indicate modest stopping-rule overhead.

The manuscript is well organized and clearly motivates cost-adjusted simple regret. It candidly reports weaker results under model mismatch, including CIFAR-100, ImageNet16-120, and unknown-cost Adult, rather than hiding these cases. LLM assistance is disclosed, and no material research-ethics issue is apparent.
weaknesses: The central theoretical presentation is not sound as written. Lemma 1 defines alpha_t using observations through t but claims alpha_t(x_t) is the expected improvement used to select x_t; in the stated noiseless setting, x_t has already been observed and this quantity is zero. Equations (15)–(16) likewise condition on F_{t-1} while using alpha_t. These should apparently use alpha_{t-1}(x_t), requiring a consistent re-indexing of the lemma, stopping time, and proof.

Theorem 2 claims a bound on cost-adjusted regret, but its proof ends after bounding cumulative cost by C+U and never establishes the displayed bound including terminal simple regret. A short telescoping argument may repair this, and optional stopping can likely be replaced by a carefully justified monotone-convergence argument, but the submitted proof does not currently prove its headline statement.

The analyzed rule differs materially from the evaluated implementation. Experiments initialize with 2(d+1) samples rather than one, impose a stabilization period and debounce requirement, and in 8D apply a 20-step moving average. These interventions can force evaluations after EI falls below cost, so the theorem does not cover the reported algorithm. This also contradicts the prominent claim of being free of heuristic tuning.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or artifact is identified, and the lengths of the stabilization period and debounce window are not specified despite being essential algorithmic parameters. Some baseline choices are also altered, such as SRGap-med's empirical threshold, without a sensitivity study, making comparative robustness difficult to assess.

The budget corollary has limited operational support: it requires the generally unavailable prior quantity U, assumes B>C, and does not address the multi-point initialization or practical stopping modifications. The empirical substitution U=50 is heuristic rather than a demonstrated implementation of the promised principled calibration.

Originality and significance are moderate rather than exceptional. The rule reduces to the natural myopic condition EI(x) <= c(x) for every x, closely related to previously discussed acquisition-threshold rules; the PBGI equivalence is elegant but elementary. The experiments suggest usefulness, but the theoretical and reproducibility gaps currently outweigh that merit.

strengths: The stopping criterion has a clear economic interpretation: continue only when some point's posterior expected improvement is at least its evaluation cost. The equivalence between the PBGI and LogEIPC forms is simple, useful, and clearly derived.

The theoretical argument appears basically sound under its stated Bayesian, noiseless, exact-optimization setting. Lemma 1 establishes the key one-step inequality, and Theorem 2 correctly telescopes expected improvements to show expected cost-adjusted regret no worse than immediate stopping.

The empirical study is broad, covering matched-prior synthetic experiments, an 8-dimensional numerical-optimization setting, 35 LCBench tasks, three NATS-Bench tasks, varying cost functions and scales, unknown-cost modeling, and cost-model mismatch. Reporting 50 seeds and uncertainty bars is good practice.

The paper is generally well organized and candidly reports important failures: the recommended pairs underperform on roughly 25% of LCBench datasets and degrade on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet16-120 under apparent model misspecification.

The method has low stopping-rule overhead and could be practically useful when objective improvement and evaluation cost can be expressed in common units. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent, and the LLM-use disclosure is appropriate.
weaknesses: The main guarantee is quite weak: it only says the method is no worse in Bayes expectation than stopping immediately. This follows directly from requiring one-step posterior expected improvement to exceed cost and does not establish proximity to the Bayes-optimal policy, an oracle stopping rule, or even a nontrivial improvement over immediate stopping. It also depends on a correctly specified posterior and exact acquisition optimization, precisely the assumptions violated in the more realistic experiments.

Originality is limited. The manuscript itself shows that the rule is equivalent to an existing expected-improvement stopping rule and derives the PBGI version from the classical Pandora's Box stopping condition. The principal novelty is therefore the cost-aware synthesis, pairing, and elementary bound rather than a substantially new stopping principle.

The practical algorithm is not adequately reproducible. The paper introduces a stabilization period and a debounce requirement but describes both only as 'several' evaluations or iterations, without giving exact values. No source-code or repository information is provided. These omissions are consequential because the stopping time is the central experimental outcome.

The claim that the method operates 'without heuristic tuning' is undermined by its implementation: the 8D experiments apply a 20-iteration moving average, practical stopping uses stabilization and debouncing, and cost-to-objective conversion requires a user- or provider-specified scaling factor. The reported rule is therefore not simply the theorem's threshold rule.

The empirical conclusions are sensitive to modeling choices and cost scale. Representative empirical cost scales are selected partly to exclude degenerate regimes, while the method performs poorly on a substantial subset of LCBench and on two of three NATS datasets in an important regime. Attributing these failures to model misspecification is plausible but not demonstrated through diagnostics or controlled misspecification experiments.

Several evaluation choices weaken comparison clarity: SRGap-med is changed from its recommended parameter for empirical tasks; capped runs are treated as stopping at the cap; and the headline LCBench aggregation uses min-max normalization across methods, including hindsight, which can obscure absolute differences. Sensitivity analyses for baseline thresholds and the proposed rule's smoothing/debounce choices are missing.

The theoretical statement needs sharper technical conditions and edge-case handling. Compactness alone does not ensure acquisition extrema are attained without continuity assumptions; the possibility of an infinite stopping time when costs lack a positive lower bound is not explicitly formalized; and Corollary 4 requires conditions such as B>C and a valid positive scaling factor that are not stated.

Presentation is mostly clear, but the limitations are dispersed rather than systematically summarized. The paper should explicitly delimit the theory's lack of robustness to posterior misspecification, noise, approximate acquisition optimization, and uncertain costs; the unknown-cost substitution using posterior expected cost is not covered by the deterministic-cost guarantee.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant problem: adaptive stopping when Bayesian-optimization evaluations have heterogeneous costs. The proposed rule has an intuitive interpretation—continue only when some point's posterior expected improvement exceeds its evaluation cost.

The algebraic equivalence between the PBGI stopping condition and the LogEIPC threshold is clear, and the telescoping expected-improvement argument behind Theorem 2 is plausible for the idealized, correctly specified noiseless Bayesian setting.

The evaluation is broad in raw scale: 1D and 8D synthetic problems, 35 LCBench datasets, three NATS-Bench datasets, multiple cost regimes, 50 seeds, and several acquisition-function/stopping-rule combinations. Error bars, per-dataset appendix results, failure-to-stop counts, runtime measurements, and negative results under model mismatch are useful.

The manuscript is generally readable and visually polished. Experimental parameters and proxy-cost constructions are documented in substantial detail, and the authors disclose both LLM assistance and several empirical failure cases.
No material research-ethics concern is apparent: the work uses established synthetic and public benchmark data, and its LLM-use disclosure is appropriately explicit.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is much weaker than its framing suggests. Theorem 2 essentially formalizes the one-step accounting identity that repeatedly purchasing evaluations whose conditional expected improvement is at least their cost cannot be worse in expectation than stopping initially. As the authors acknowledge in footnote 5, this applies to any policy satisfying that condition; it does not establish near-optimality, a nontrivial regret rate, or an advantage over competing cost-aware rules in the correlated setting.

The experiments do not implement the algorithm covered by the theorem. The theorem begins from one point and stops as soon as the threshold is crossed, whereas experiments force 2(d+1) initial evaluations, impose a stabilization period, use debouncing, and in 8D replace the current signal with a 20-step moving average. These modifications can continue sampling when expected improvement is below cost, directly breaking Lemma 1 and the claimed no-worse-than-immediate guarantee. The paper neither proves a guarantee for this practical algorithm nor clearly separates its claims from those for the idealized rule.

The theorem is stated under insufficient technical conditions. Compactness alone does not ensure that an arbitrary random function attains a minimum, that acquisition extrema exist, or that the relevant quantities are measurable and integrable. The proof also manipulates a potentially unbounded stopping time without supplying the truncation or convergence argument needed to avoid circularity with the subsequent finite-termination corollary. These issues may be repairable but matter for the paper's main formal claim.

The claim of adaptation 'without heuristic tuning' is overstated. The objective-to-cost conversion factor lambda encodes a consequential user utility choice; the practical method additionally needs an initial no-stop period, debounce length, and, in 8D, a moving-average window. Lambda values are selected to avoid degenerate regimes, but sensitivity to these practical choices is not systematically evaluated.

The empirical evidence is less decisive than the breadth suggests. The method is consistently poor on roughly one quarter of LCBench datasets, is visibly suboptimal on two of three principal NATS-Bench datasets, and can lose to Immediate or simple heuristics under unknown costs. Attributing failures largely to small datasets or model misspecification is speculative, especially because two prominent failures have 32,769 and 50,000 examples and no diagnostic evidence is presented.

The main LCBench summary uses min-max normalization based on extrema across all evaluated pairs, including the hindsight oracle. This can distort cross-dataset aggregation, and the paper reports no average ranks, paired statistical tests, confidence intervals over dataset-level differences, or win/tie/loss analysis to substantiate 'usually matches or outperforms.' Baseline parameters are mostly fixed from prior work, one is manually altered, and all rules receive unusual smoothing in 8D, leaving fairness and robustness unclear.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The manuscript gives many implementation details but provides no code or artifact link, despite relying on numerous custom choices, proxy-cost regressions, stabilization/debounce behavior, benchmark preprocessing, and acquisition optimization. Exact reproduction from the PDF alone would be difficult.

Limitations are scattered rather than treated systematically. The method and guarantee assume noiseless, correctly specified posterior expectations; noisy observations, severe GP misspecification, multi-fidelity, and batched evaluation are deferred to future work even though misspecification already causes substantial failures. Overall, the idea is useful and the paper has clear merits, but the gap between the clean idealized guarantee and the tuned practical method, together with limited novelty and mixed empirical results, currently outweighs them.

strengths: Soundness: The stopping condition has a clear decision-theoretic interpretation—stop when no unevaluated point has posterior expected improvement exceeding its cost—and its equivalence under PBGI and LogEIPC is derived cleanly. Lemma 1 and the telescoping argument in Theorem 2 appear technically sound under the stated noiseless, correctly specified Bayesian model.

Originality and significance: Cost-aware adaptive stopping is practically important and comparatively underexplored. Connecting Pandora’s Box stopping to LogEIPC supplies useful conceptual unification, while the resulting automatic rule could reduce unnecessary expensive evaluations.

Evaluation: The paper studies acquisition–stopping-rule pairs rather than isolating the stopping rule unrealistically. It includes matched-prior synthetic experiments, an 8D setting with imperfect acquisition optimization, 35 LCBench tasks, three NATS-Bench tasks, 50 seeds, several cost scales, unknown-cost and cost-model-mismatch variants, and multiple established baselines.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. Definitions, assumptions, proofs, baseline parameters, cost proxies, and extensive per-dataset results are provided. The figures make the cost–quality trade-off and stopping behavior understandable.

Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly report systematic failures on several LCBench datasets and two NATS-Bench tasks, relate them to model mismatch, and avoid hiding unfavorable per-dataset results behind the aggregate plot. No material ethical concern is apparent, and LLM assistance is disclosed.
weaknesses: The central guarantee is limited: it only establishes expected cost-adjusted regret no worse than stopping immediately after the first evaluation. This is a weak baseline and gives neither near-optimality nor comparison with a competitive stopping policy in the correlated setting. The paper sometimes presents this result more strongly than its content warrants.

There is a consequential theory–practice gap. The theorem covers the exact rule beginning from one initial point under model correctness, whereas experiments use 2(d+1) initial samples and practical modifications such as a stabilization period, debouncing, and—in 8D—a 20-iteration moving average. These modified rules are not covered by the guarantee.

The claim of stopping “without heuristic tuning” is weakened by those practical safeguards. The stabilization duration and debounce requirement are not precisely specified, and there is no sensitivity analysis for these choices or the moving-average window. Their effect on stopping time and comparisons could be substantial.

Empirical conclusions are encouraging but not fully decisive. Representative cost scales are explicitly selected to avoid degenerate regimes; some baseline parameters are altered, notably SRGap-med; no sensitivity analysis or paired statistical tests are reported; and the main LCBench aggregation uses method-dependent min–max normalization, which can obscure absolute differences. The appendix mitigates the last issue with unnormalized per-task plots.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or repository is identified, and some implementation details needed to reproduce the practical stopping logic are missing. The benchmarks and most model settings are documented, but the unspecified stabilization/debounce procedure prevents exact reconstruction.

The limitations discussion is distributed rather than systematic. In particular, the paper should distinguish more explicitly among failure from GP misspecification, cost-model misspecification, and acquisition-optimization error, and should discuss noisy observations, where both the rule and proof may behave differently.
